title: What God Has Placed in Your Hands
shortDescription: Many times we search for purpose by looking at what we still do not have, when an important part of our calling begins with what God has already placed in our hands. This five-day journey will help you recognize gifts, time, relationships, resources, and opportunities as things entrusted to you that can be stewarded faithfully. You will learn to let go of comparison, value small beginnings, serve with what you have, and turn everyday responsibility into a concrete expression of purpose.
learning: Recognize the gifts, resources, relationships, and opportunities that are already part of your responsibility
Understand purpose through stewardship and not only through great future goals
Learn to value and develop small beginnings without despising them
Distinguish between comparison and faithful stewardship of what you have received
Discover how to place what you have at the service of others and God's work
gains: Greater clarity about resources and abilities you may have underestimated
Less frustration from comparing yourself with what others have
More willingness to begin with what is available
A practical view of purpose applied to everyday life
A greater sense of responsibility and service regarding what God has entrusted to you

days.title: Look First at What You Already Have
days.text:
When we think about purpose, we tend to look at what we lack. We lack money, experience, contacts, time, an opportunity, or a platform. That perspective can cause us to overlook resources that are already present and could become a starting point.

In Exodus, God asks Moses what he has in his hand. In 2 Kings, Elisha asks a widow what she has in her house. In both accounts, the answer begins with something that seemed small or insufficient. The emphasis is not on idealizing what little there is, but on recognizing that God can begin to work with what is available.

Perhaps you already have an ability, an experience, a relationship, a free hour, or a resource that can be used intentionally. Purpose does not always begin when you receive something new. Often it begins when you learn to see differently what has already been entrusted to you.
days.internalize: Before saying, “I do not have enough,” take inventory of what is already present in your life.
days.prayer: Lord, open my eyes to recognize what You have already placed in my hands. Free me from despising resources, abilities, or opportunities because they seem small. Teach me to steward them faithfully. Amen.
days.action: Make a list of five things you already have that could serve a purpose: time, skills, experiences, relationships, knowledge, or material resources.

days.title: You Do Not Need to Have What Someone Else Has
days.text:
Comparison can distract you from your own responsibility. While you are watching someone else's talent, influence, or opportunities, you may neglect what you are actually responsible for developing.

When Peter wanted to know what would happen to John, Jesus brought him back to his own following. Paul explains that the body has different members and that this diversity is intentional. Not everyone receives the same function, but everyone can contribute.

Your purpose does not need to look like someone else's in order to be legitimate. Comparison can lead you to despise what you have or chase a task that was never entrusted to you. Maturity asks less, “Why don't I have that?” and more, “How can I be faithful with this?”
days.internalize: Comparison looks sideways. Stewardship looks at what is in front of you and asks how to manage it well.
days.prayer: Father, free me from measuring my life by the measure of others. Give me gratitude for what You have entrusted to each person and faithfulness to develop what You placed in my hands. Amen.
days.action: Identify one comparison that frequently distracts you. Then write down one responsibility or gift of your own to which you will return your attention.

days.title: Small Things Also Require Faithfulness
days.text:
We may think we will be more responsible when we have something bigger: more time, more money, more influence, or a better opportunity. But Jesus connects faithfulness with the way we manage small things.

Zechariah asks who despises the day of small beginnings. That warning is still relevant. Many projects, callings, and abilities begin modestly. Before they grow, they need consistency, learning, and care.

Purpose is not demonstrated only in major moments. It is also built through repeated habits: keeping your word, finishing what you started, caring for a skill, managing a resource well, or serving when no one is watching. Small things can become a place of preparation for greater responsibilities.
days.internalize: Do not ask only, “When will this grow?” Also ask, “Am I taking good care of the small version I have today?”
days.prayer: Lord, teach me to be faithful in small things. Form in me consistency, discipline, and gratitude so I can care well for what seems simple today. Amen.
days.action: Choose one small responsibility you have treated carelessly. Define one concrete way to handle it better during the next seven days.

days.title: What You Received Can Also Bless Others
days.text:
A resource finds a deeper dimension of purpose when it stops serving only the person who possesses it. Peter teaches that each person should steward what they have received in service to others.

That includes more than money. You can share knowledge, time, experience, hospitality, creativity, listening, organization, or a professional skill. The question is not only what you have, but what good what you have can produce when it is placed at the service of someone else.

Serving also helps you discover purpose. When you put an ability into motion, you begin to observe where there is fruit, which needs connect with your heart, and which skills are worth continuing to develop. Many answers appear after you begin contributing.
days.internalize: Make this shift: from “How can I use this for myself?” to “How can this also become good for someone else?”
days.prayer: God, thank You for everything I have received. I do not want to keep it only for myself. Show me how to turn my resources and abilities into service, help, and blessing for others. Amen.
days.action: Choose one of the resources you identified on the first day and use it this week to benefit one person in a concrete way.

days.title: Steward Today What You Want to See Multiplied Tomorrow
days.text:
The parable of the talents shows people receiving different amounts, but being evaluated by their faithfulness with what they received. The emphasis is not on comparing amounts, but on responding responsibly to the trust that was given.

What God has placed in your hands may need development. A talent without practice remains limited. An opportunity without consistency is lost. A relationship without care weakens. A project without discipline can remain only an intention.

Multiplication does not always mean more fame, money, or reach. It can mean greater maturity, greater usefulness, greater excellence, or deeper impact. Your responsibility is not to guarantee extraordinary results, but to work diligently and entrust the outcome to God.

Living with purpose means learning to say, “This is what I have today, and I want to steward it in a way worthy of the One who entrusted it to me.”
days.internalize: Close this journey with a stewardship question: “If I cared for this faithfully for a year, what could it become?”
days.prayer: Lord, I want to steward well what You placed in my hands. Give me discipline to develop it, humility to use it in service to others, and freedom to leave the results in your hands. Amen.
days.action: Choose one ability, resource, or responsibility you want to develop during the next 30 days. Define one concrete and measurable weekly practice to care for it.
